Reproductive investment in Lethrinus ornatus was assessed through field collections conducted during the pre-spawning aggregation period in the central Great Barrier Reef. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 6% [GSI = 6%] across the sampled population under the ambient thermal regime of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. A small, spherical fertilised ovum measuring roughly 0.7 millimetres in diameter was described from plankton tows. Based on this recorded egg diameter, the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value that reflects the tiny mass of the yolk-laden egg at the moment of fertilisation and which underscores the extreme fecundity required to offset high egg and early larval mortality in a pelagic spawning environment.

Growth trajectories for this species were reconstructed from length-frequency data and validated against otolith readings from both commercial catch samples and dedicated research surveys. The ultimate total length, representing the asymptotic maximum size attained by older individuals in undisturbed populations, was estimated at 45 cm [Li = 45 cm]. This terminal size is moderate compared to the maximum lengths reported for other members of the Lethrinus genus, some of which surpass 80 cm total length. Corresponding to this length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual was calculated using a standard length–weight relationship and found to be 1873 g [Wwi = 1873 g]. This value describes the upper bound of somatic mass that a reproductively senescent adult might achieve after many years of growth. The length–weight relationship used for this conversion was derived from a large sample of specimens spanning the full size range, and the resulting 1873 g value aligns well with the heaviest individuals recorded in local fishery-independent surveys.

Sexual maturation in the ornate emperor proceeds at a size considerably smaller than the asymptotic maximum, as is typical for a species that begins to reproduce well before somatic growth plateaus. The total length at puberty, defined here as the size at which fifty percent of individuals display active gametogenesis, was determined to be 20 cm [Lp = 20 cm]. This relatively modest length at the onset of reproductive maturity implies that individuals can begin contributing to the next generation after only a few years of growth. The corresponding wet weight at puberty derived from the same species-specific length–weight conversion is 161.8 g [Wwp = 161.8 g]. This body mass at first reproductive competence is substantially lower than the ultimate wet weight of 1873 g, reflecting a life-history strategy in which early reproduction is favoured at the expense of maximal somatic size, a pattern often associated with moderate to high natural mortality rates in coral reef fishes.

Longevity records for Lethrinus ornatus were assembled from both tag-recapture studies and annual otolith increment analyses conducted in waters with a mean annual water temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. The oldest documented individual in these datasets reached a life span of 5110 days [am = 5110 days], which is equivalent to approximately 14 years at a temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. This maximum age places the ornate emperor among the longer-lived members of its genus, though several congeneric species in cooler, higher-latitude waters are known to exceed 20 years. The consistency of the otolith-derived age estimates with tag-recapture data lends confidence to the 5110 day figure, which represents the total duration from egg fertilisation to natural death.

The ecological role of Lethrinus ornatus as a benthic carnivore was examined through stomach content analysis of specimens collected across a range of habitat types, including seagrass beds and coral rubble zones. Juveniles, defined as post-metamorphic individuals smaller than the size at puberty, feed predominantly on small crustaceans and polychaetes, while adults shift toward a diet dominated by molluscs, decapods, and echinoderms. This ontogenetic dietary shift is accompanied by a corresponding change in jaw morphology and tooth structure, reflecting the greater mechanical demands of processing hard-shelled prey. Field observations of spawning behaviour indicate that adults form loose aggregations on reef slopes and outer shelf edges during the summer months, releasing buoyant, transparent pellets that drift with prevailing currents for several days before hatching. Pelagic larval duration is estimated to be between 25 and 35 days, after which the postflexion larvae settle into shallow seagrass nurseries. An asymptotic total length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], a gonadosomatic index of 6% [GSI = 6%], and a maximum longevity of 5110 days [am = 5110 days] at 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C] were recorded for this species.
